scenes.text: The longest questions, worth six to nine marks, can decide a band. In six years of NESA's marking feedback for Chemistry and Biology, every report flagged answers that ignored the stimulus or copied it without explaining it, and more than half flagged judgements without reasons. So here's how to plan a long answer in a minute, build it one idea per paragraph, use the stimulus, and finish with a judgement when the verb asks.

Long answers usually aren't marked by ticking separate points. A marker reads the whole answer and places it in a band. In recent guidelines, the top band for this kind of question asks for detailed use of the stimulus and a well-supported judgement. So the target isn't more words. It's every demand covered, with evidence, in an order a marker can follow.

Here's an HSC-style Biology question. Region R's measles vaccination coverage fell after some clinics closed, and a school catch-up program began in twenty eighteen. The table gives coverage and cases from twenty ten to twenty twenty two. Seven marks. Read it, and plan what you'd write. Take a full minute if you like. Pause here to answer.

Step one: take the question apart. There are two verbs. Analyse the data to explain the change in cases, and assess the catch-up program. There's a constraint: refer to immunity in individuals and in the population. And there's the stimulus, which you're expected to use. That's four demands, so write four small ticks in the margin, and tick each one as you cover it.

Step two: assess asks for a judgement, so decide it first. Here, the program probably contributed, with a limit. Then jot one line per paragraph. Vaccine, memory cells. Ninety five per cent, herd immunity. Coverage fell, cases rose. Catch-up, cases fell, plus a limit. Next to each line, write the number from the table it'll use. That's your plan, and it takes about a minute.

Now build each paragraph the same way. Make the point. Give the evidence from the stimulus, with numbers. Explain the biology that links them. Then link back to the question. Take paragraph three. Coverage fell from ninety five to eighty seven per cent. With fewer people immune, an infected person met more susceptible people, so chains of transmission kept going, and cases rose from eight to three hundred and ten. So the fall in coverage explains the outbreak.

The first two paragraphs cover the constraint. One for the individual: the vaccine presents measles antigens without the disease, so the body makes memory cells, and a later infection meets a fast secondary response. One for the population: when coverage is near the ninety five per cent target, most people are immune, so the virus rarely finds a new host, which fits the low cases of twenty ten and twenty twelve. One idea per paragraph keeps each link easy to see.

Using the stimulus means more than copying it. A weak answer says cases went up, then down. A strong one picks the values that matter, compares them, and says what they mean: coverage dropped below the ninety five per cent target, and that's when cases climbed. Quote the number, then interpret it.

Assess asks for a judgement, so state it in your first line, and come back to it at the end. Before the program, from twenty sixteen to twenty eighteen, cases had already fallen from three hundred and ten to a hundred and eighty. After it began, coverage rose from eighty nine to ninety five per cent, and cases fell to six. These data can't separate the program's effect from other changes. So the fair judgement is: the program probably contributed, though we can't say how much. A judgement with its condition is stronger than a bare yes.

Put two answers side by side. The weak one describes the trend, explains vaccination in general, and ends with, so the program was good because vaccines are important. It covers one verb, uses no numbers, and its judgement has no reasons. The strong one covers both verbs and both kinds of immunity, uses the table's values, and judges the program with a condition. Same science, different band.

Your turn. Do the one in your subject, or both. Biology first. A ward started hand hygiene training in July, and in the same month a new cleaning routine. Compliance and infection rates are on screen. The question says evaluate the training program, for six marks. Don't write the answer. Write the plan: the demands, your judgement, and one line per paragraph. Pause here to answer.

Judgement first: probably effective, but not proven. Line one: hand hygiene breaks the contact link. Line two: compliance rose from forty five to eighty two per cent while infections fell from six to two point five. Line three: the cleaning routine started the same month, so training can't take all the credit. The habit to drop: starting to write without a plan.

Now Chemistry. The question: evaluate the use of soap for washing clothes in a town with hard water. A student explains the scum, the wasted soap and the grey deposits, and that soap is renewable and breaks down readily. Her last line is, overall, soap has advantages and disadvantages. Rewrite that line so it makes a judgement. Pause here to answer.

A judgement takes a side, and gives the reason. For example: in this hard-water town, soap is a poor choice for washing clothes, because calcium ions turn much of it into scum, which wastes soap and marks the fabric, even though soap is renewable. Advantages and disadvantages, with no decision, is the trap. It's a summary, not a judgement.

So, for a long answer: take the question apart, and tick each demand. If the verb asks for a judgement, decide it first. Plan one line per paragraph, with the evidence it'll use. Build each paragraph as point, evidence, explain, link. And when the verb asks, end with the judgement and its condition. Next in Biology: practise evaluating disease control strategies.
